title: Tilda and the Lost Mouse
markdown:
Tucked between the mossy roots of a pine that reached for the stars lived Tilda, a young witch whose spells were as gentle as a butterfly’s wing. Her cottage hummed with lavender and simmering herbs, and her friendly mountain lantern cast a honey-gold glow that made the shadows dance away.

One evening, as Tilda stirred a pot of sleepy-time stew, smelling of moonlight and dreams, she heard a tiny frantic scrabbling. It wasn’t the familiar rustle of a beetle or the soft thump of a dropped spell book. It was a small worried sound, like a little leaf caught in a sudden blustery sigh of wind.

Tilda settled down like a falling leaf and peered under her armchair, its cushions soft and worn. There, quivering like a dewdrop on a spider’s web, was a little mouse. He was so small his whiskers seemed as long as his body, and his fur was the colour of a dusty acorn, blending perfectly with the cottage floor. He looked quite lost, tiny paws tucked underneath him as if he were trying to melt into the rug.

Tilda knelt, her starry robe pooling around her like a spilled midnight sky. “Oh, you poor little thing,” she said, her voice as soft as the down of a young owl. “You’ve strayed from your family, haven’t you? It’s a big wide world for such a little creature.”

The mouse gave a tiny shaky squeak, barely audible above the gentle bubbling of the stew.

“Don’t you worry,” Tilda assured him, her eyes sparkling like tiny constellations. “We’ll get you home. What’s your name, little one?”

He blinked his bead-like eyes, which seemed to hold a universe of worry. “Pipkin,” he squeaked, a whisper of a rustle, like leaves skittering across a path.

Tilda smiled. “Pipkin. That’s a very nice name. And Pipkin, I’m Tilda. I live right here in the Misty Crags. We can help you find your way. My cottage is safe, and so are the woods outside, especially with my lantern.”

Pipkin trembled a little more, his whole body a tiny quake. The world outside Tilda’s warm cottage seemed very big and very dark, and he was sure he’d never find his way back.

“It’s alright,” Tilda said, scooping him up very gently, her hands as soft as moss. She held him for a moment, feeling his tiny heart beat like a hummingbird’s wings against her palm. “My mountain lantern will light our way. It knows all the paths, you see. It remembers the way the moonbeams fall on the forest floor.” Pipkin settled a little, finding the warmth of Tilda’s hand and the steady glow of the lantern quite comforting. The lantern knew the way, or so Tilda liked to tell it, and tonight it would have to prove it.

Tilda carefully placed Pipkin into a soft moss-lined pouch she wore around her neck. The moss was gathered from the shadiest parts of the Crags, and it felt like sleeping on a cloud. Pipkin’s little nose poked out, and he seemed to feel much braver there, peeking at Tilda’s friendly face and the familiar glow of her many little jars filled with sparkling dust and dried flowers. She picked up her mountain lantern, which pulsed with a gentle steady light, brighter than any star. “Ready, Pipkin?”

Pipkin gave a determined little nod, his whiskers twitching with a touch of bravery. The lantern knew the way.

And so Tilda and Pipkin stepped out into the cool crisp night air. The whispering pines stood tall and silent, their needles rustling softly, sharing secrets with the wind. The moon, a sliver of pearly light, hung high above, watching over the sleepy mountains like a gentle eye. Tilda’s lantern bobbed along, a friendly little sun in the dimness, casting dancing shadows that looked like playful sprites on the forest floor.

They hadn’t gone far, not even past the first cluster of sleepy bluebells, when they heard a peculiar humming sound. It was like a bumblebee wearing spectacles, a gentle buzz mixed with the rustle of many papers being shuffled. Around a bend in the path, where the moonlight dappled the ground, they saw her. It was Morwenna Bright, the wizard who lived on the highest peak, known throughout the Misty Crags for her kindness and her rather enthusiastic collection of maps. Morwenna had maps of everything: maps of the clouds shaped like animals, maps of lost socks that vanished from the laundry, maps of the taste of sunshine on a summer’s day.

Morwenna squinted at them, her long star-dusted beard tickling her chin and making her look like a benevolent fluffy cloud. “Well, hello there, Tilda,” she boomed, her voice like pebbles rolling down a gentle slope. “And who is this little fellow peeking out from your pouch?”

“Pipkin,” Tilda said, her voice bright and clear. “He’s lost his way home, and I’m helping him find his cosy burrow.”

“Lost, you say?” Morwenna tutted, a sound of deep concern. She began to rummage through her enormous bulging satchel, pulling out a rolled-up scroll. “Hmm. Most unfortunate. Let me see. I have a map here of all the mouse-holes in the Crags. Ah, yes.” She unfurled it with a flourish. It looked very much like all her other maps, covered in squiggly lines and tiny illegible notes that seemed to dance on the parchment. “Pipkin, my dear boy, where abouts do you live?”

Pipkin, peeking from Tilda’s pouch, squeaked, “Near the big twisty oak tree by the Sparkle Stream. It has the best acorns.”

Morwenna tapped her chin with a long bony finger. “Sparkle Stream… twisty oak… that sounds familiar. Ah. This map says… no, wait. Is that a cloud or a badger’s burrow? Oh dear, this one seems to be a map of my breakfast yesterday. I distinctly remember a rather good blueberry muffin. Never mind.” She pulled out another, even larger map, this one unfurling to reveal a dizzying array of lines. “This one is definitely it. See, Tilda? It shows a little red X right… here.” She pointed to a spot that looked suspiciously like a smudge of ink, or perhaps a very surprised ladybug.

Tilda peered at it, her brow furrowed slightly. It looked rather like a very fluffy sheep, or perhaps a particularly bumpy cloud that had decided to take a nap on the map. “Are you sure, Morwenna?” she asked gently. “It looks a little bit like a picture of your favourite teacup, the one with the little bluebirds on it.”

Morwenna blinked, her eyes widening behind her spectacles. “Does it? Good heavens, it might. I do have a rather lovely teacup. Perhaps this is a map of my teacup collection. So many maps, you see, they all start to look alike after a while. It’s like trying to tell one snowflake from another.” She chuckled, a sound like pebbles rolling down a hill, warm and friendly.

Pipkin wriggled slightly in the pouch. He was starting to feel a little more worried again. Morwenna’s maps were interesting to look at, with all their swirls and dots, but they didn’t seem to be pointing him towards his warm bed or his mama. The lantern knew the way, Tilda thought, better than a breakfast map.

Tilda, ever patient and observant, looked around. The air here smelled faintly of damp earth and sweet clover, a familiar scent that always made her feel calm. Her lantern’s light played on the bark of the trees, highlighting patterns that looked like sleepy faces. And then she noticed something, or rather, she heard something. “Morwenna,” she said gently, “Pipkin said his home is near the Sparkle Stream. Do you hear that?”

They both stopped and listened. And there it was, a faint tinkling sound, like tiny silver bells being shaken by the wind. It was the Sparkle Stream, much closer than Morwenna’s map suggested, its water bubbling merrily over smooth stones. And just beyond it, illuminated by Tilda’s steady lantern light, was a truly magnificent twisty oak tree, its branches reaching out like welcoming arms.

“Oh my goodness.” Morwenna’s eyes wide with surprise. “The Sparkle Stream. And the twisty oak. Why, Pipkin, my dear boy, your home is right over there.” She gestured with a flourish, nearly dropping her teacup map in her excitement. “It seems my map wasn’t quite accurate. More of a suggestion, really.” She gave Tilda a sheepish grin, the stars in her beard twinkling. “Perhaps I should stick to mapping my sock drawer. At least I know where all my socks are, even if they do like to hide in pairs.”

Pipkin wriggled with pure excitement, his little nose twitching wildly. He could see a tiny opening at the base of the twisty oak, snuggled amongst the roots like a secret doorway. It looked so cosy and familiar, exactly as he remembered it.

Tilda carefully took Pipkin out of her pouch. She knelt down so he could easily reach his home. “Here we are, Pipkin,” she said softly, her smile as warm as her hearth fire. “Your home. Safe and sound.”

Pipkin gave Tilda a grateful squeak and a tiny nudge of his head against her finger. Then, with a burst of happy energy, he scurried down towards the oak. He disappeared into the cosy opening, and a moment later a few other tiny noses poked out from the darkness, followed by a flurry of happy squeaks. Pipkin was home, surrounded by his family.

Tilda watched them, a warm feeling spreading through her chest, like sunshine after a gentle rain. Morwenna Bright stood beside her, humming a cheerful tune and carefully rolling up her maps, perhaps to be sorted later. “Well, Tilda,” she said, her voice full of quiet wonder. “That was a fine adventure for such a little mouse.”

As the first blush of dawn painted the sky in soft shades of rose and gold, chasing away the last of the night’s indigo, Tilda and Morwenna turned back towards their homes. The whispering pines seemed to sigh contentedly. The mountain lantern in Tilda’s hand cast a contented honey-gold glow. The lantern knew the way, and the Sparkle Stream had said so first, which was how you knew a lost mouse could outshine a breakfast map.
characters: Tilda (young witch of the Misty Crags), Pipkin (a dusty-acorn mouse)
